intro: Pick up a printed Qur'an and you hold a book that Muslims say began as a voice. This unit looks at the book as a made thing: how its 114 chapters are arranged, why the short ones ring like songs and the long ones read like law, what the strange letters at the top of some chapters are, and how the whole thing was gathered, written, dotted, printed and recited over fourteen centuries.

You will learn the words readers use: surah and ayah, juz' and hizb, Meccan and Medinan, tajwid and qira'at. You will meet the people tradition names, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Bakr, Uthman, and the scholars who added the marks. You will also meet the evidence historians use, including two pages of parchment in an English library that turned out to be older than anyone expected.

This is the study of a scripture in a public school. We describe what the Qur'an says and how Muslims and scholars read it; we do not decide whether it is true. By the end you should be able to open the book to any surah, say what kind of chapter it is, and explain how the words on the page got there.
bigQuestion: How is the Qur'an built, and how did a text spoken aloud in Arabia become the book Muslims read and recite today?

timeline.t: By Muslim tradition, the first words are revealed: 'Read,' Qur'an 96:1–5
Meccan surahs: short, rhymed, oaths and warnings of the Last Day
The hijra to Medina; the longer Medinan surahs of law and community begin
The Prophet Muhammad dies; the text lives in memory and scattered writings
After the battle of Yamama, Abu Bakr has Zayd ibn Thabit collect the text
Uthman sends standard copies to the main cities
The oldest surviving manuscripts are written in bare Hijazi script
Dots and vowel marks are added to the script
Ibn Mujahid dies, having fixed the seven authoritative readings
The Cairo edition sets the standard printed text
The Sana'a manuscripts are found in Yemen
The Birmingham leaves are radiocarbon-dated to 568–645 CE

words.d: a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114
a verse; the Arabic word also means a sign
one of 30 equal parts for reading the Qur'an in a month
a surah tradition places before 622; usually short, rhymed and about judgment
a surah tradition places after the hijra; usually long and about law and community
rhymed prose, the ringing line endings of many Meccan surahs
the disconnected letters, such as Alif Lam Mim, that open 29 surahs
a short teaching comparison, in Arabic a mathal, like the spider's house
a person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
the standard written text made under the caliph Uthman c. 650
the accepted readings, or ways of reciting, the Qur'an, such as Hafs and Warsh
the rules for reciting the Qur'an exactly

test.q: How many surahs does the Qur'an have?
test.why: There are 114 surahs; 30 is the number of juz' and about 6,236 the number of ayahs.

test.q: The name Al-Baqarah, The Cow, for Surah 2 comes from
choices: the tribe that first heard it
a short story inside the surah
the shape of its first letter
test.why: Most surah names come from a memorable word or story inside; the cow story is 2:67–73.

test.q: A hizb is best described as
test.why: Each of the 30 juz' has two hizb, for 60 in all.

test.q: Which is a feature of Meccan surahs?
choices: oaths by the sun, the night or the morning
test.why: Opening oaths and short rhymed lines are typical of Mecca; law belongs to Medina.

test.q: The refrain repeated 31 times in Surah 55 asks
choices: which of the favors of your Lord you deny
test.why: Ar-Rahman's return line is 'Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?'

test.q: The mainstream Muslim position on the meaning of the muqatta'at is that
choices: they are the names of the scribes
their meaning is not known for certain
they are the first verse of the Qur'an
they were added in Cairo in 1924
test.why: Al-Tabari listed many views and settled on none; that remains the mainstream position.

test.q: Which surah do Muslims recite in every unit of daily prayer?
test.why: Al-Fatiha, the Seven Oft-Repeated, is recited in every rak'ah.

test.q: By Muslim tradition, the first verses revealed were
test.why: Tradition places the first revelation at 96:1–5, near the end of the book in reading order.

test.q: What does the word Qur'an mean?
test.why: Qur'an comes from a root meaning to recite or read aloud.

test.q: Tradition says Abu Bakr ordered the text collected because
choices: many memorizers died at the battle of Yamama
test.why: After Yamama, c. 633, Umar urged Abu Bakr to gather the text before more huffaz died.

choices: the standard written text sent to the main cities c. 650
test.why: Uthman's committee, led by Zayd ibn Thabit, made the standard copies around 650.

test.q: What did radiocarbon dating show about the Birmingham leaves?
choices: The parchment was from 568 to 645 CE with 95.4 percent probability
The pages were written in Latin
The text was a different book
test.why: The 2015 test dated the animal skin; the text matches the standard Qur'an in wording.

test.q: Why does a printed Qur'an show every vowel mark?
choices: because the book is in Persian
so recitation can be exact in every sound
test.why: Ordinary Arabic omits short vowels; the Qur'an is fully marked for exact recitation.

choices: two accepted readings of the one Uthmanic text
test.why: Hafs (from Asim of Kufa) and Warsh (from Nafi of Medina) are the two most widely used qira'at.

test.q: Which statement is a historian's description rather than a Muslim belief?
choices: The text was kept by memory and writing together from an early date, as manuscripts confirm
God has promised to guard the Reminder
The Qur'an was revealed in seven modes
The angel Jibril reviewed the text with the Prophet each Ramadan
test.why: The first is a claim about evidence; the others are beliefs from the Qur'an and hadith that Muslims hold.

write.prompt: How does the Qur'an's own description of itself fit with the history of how it was written down? Cite Qur'an 96:1–5, 15:9 and 73:4 (Pickthall, 1930), and the report of Zayd ibn Thabit in al-Bukhari. Explain what each text says, and how a Muslim reader and a historian each read the story of the text's preservation.
tips: Name each text you cite by surah and ayah, and name the translator and year.
Say 'Muslims believe' or 'tradition says' for beliefs, and 'historians note' for evidence.
Compare the two readings; do not decide which is true.
Use the unit's terms: mushaf, hafiz, Uthmanic codex, qira'at, tajwid.
Keep sentences short and say one thing in each.
